design_detail: Cross-sectional SPECT study (Lancet 2001;358:1864-1869) of [123I]beta-CIT binding, recruited through flyers at Amsterdam 'rave' venues with a harm-reduction agency. Four groups recruited from the same scene: 15 people with moderate ecstasy use (up to 50 tablets lifetime), 23 with heavy use (50 tablets or more), 16 who had used at least 50 tablets and had stopped for at least a year, and 15 who said they had never used ecstasy but used other drugs. One scan per person; binding expressed as the ratio of region-of-interest counts to cerebellar counts 4 h after injection, in midbrain, thalamus and four cortical regions; analysed in a mixed linear model with group, sex, region and group-by-sex terms.
can_establish: That, in these four groups scanned once, overall and regional [123I]beta-CIT binding ratios were lower in the women with heavy use than in the women in the control group, that the moderate-use groups did not differ from controls, and that women who had stopped for a year or more had higher ratios than women currently using heavily and did not differ significantly from controls.
cannot_establish: That ecstasy caused the lower binding (no pre-use scan; the groups differ in other drug use); that the higher binding in people who had stopped is recovery (different people, scanned once, not the same people followed); that men are unaffected (the paper's own power calculation shows the male comparison could not detect the difference it looked for); or that the signal is specific to serotonin, since the tracer also binds dopamine transporters.

sample.recruitment: Flyers at venues of the Amsterdam 'rave scene', with the harm-reduction agency UNITY; controls recruited from the same community source (p. 1865).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 18-45, otherwise healthy, no psychiatric history. Group thresholds: up to 50 lifetime tablets (moderate), 50 or more (heavy), 50 or more plus at least 1 year without use (stopped). Agreed abstinence from all psychoactive drugs for at least 3 weeks, then urine screening; excluded for a positive drug screen, pregnancy, severe medical or neuropsychiatric illness, or medication binding the serotonin transporter (p. 1865).
sample.demographics: Age 22.7-29.3 years by subgroup; men 3.1 years older than women (95% CI 0.6-5.6). Verbal IQ (Dutch adult reading test) 102.0-112.2, no group difference (p=0.10). Current depression in 11 of 69 participants, no group difference (p=0.86) (Table 1, p. 1865).
sample.attrition: Not applicable: one scan per person, no follow-up.
sample.selection_effects: Groups are self-selected by their own drug histories and recruited in one scene; the group that had stopped is made up of people who both used heavily and then stopped, which may differ systematically from those who continued. Exposure is self-reported, with only a urine screen at entry.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported drug history questionnaire (validated against urine testing in a Dutch survey, 93% agreement, n=594, as the authors cite, p. 1868); urine enzyme immunoassay before enrolment (p. 1865).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Reported means (Table 2, p. 1865): duration 4.1-4.6 years in all three ecstasy groups; usual dose 1.4 (SD 0.5) tablets in the moderate group, 2.2 (0.7) in the heavy group, 2.1 (1.0) in those who had stopped; lifetime tablets 28.6 (17.8), 530.0 (621.1) and 268.1 (614.3). Route not stated (tablets).
exposure.polysubstance: All groups used other drugs. Amphetamine use in the past 3 months differed between groups (p=0.04) and cocaine use nearly so (p=0.09); the ecstasy groups reported more of both than controls. Cannabis, alcohol and tobacco did not differ by group (Table 1, p. 1865). The authors argue that none of these is a known human serotonin toxin (p. 1868).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 3 weeks from all psychoactive drugs, self-reported and checked with one urine screen. Time since last tablet: 3.6 (SD 5.9) months (moderate), 2.3 (2.4) months (heavy), 29.0 (20.4) months (stopped) (Table 2, p. 1865).

comparison.controls: 15 people recruited from the same subculture who said they had never used ecstasy but used other drugs (p. 1865).
comparison.matching: Not individually matched; groups did not differ in age, verbal IQ, alcohol, tobacco or cannabis use, but did differ in amphetamine use.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use scan and no measure of serotonin transporter levels before use; the authors note that people with low transporter density might be more likely to use ecstasy (p. 1868).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Controls used other recreational drugs but reported no amphetamine or cocaine use in the past 3 months (Table 1, p. 1865).

outcomes.instruments: [123I]beta-CIT SPECT, 12-detector brain-dedicated scanner, resolution about 7.5 mm; binding ratio = region counts / cerebellar counts, 4 h after injection of about 140 MBq; regions of interest placed from a standard template by an investigator unaware of the participant's history (p. 1866).
outcomes.validity_norms: The tracer binds both serotonin and dopamine transporters; the authors argue that at 4 h in these regions binding is predominantly serotonergic, and note that striatal ratios at 24 h did not differ between groups (p. 1868). No normative values.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Neurotoxic effect' is operationalized as a lower binding ratio; 'reversibility' as a higher ratio in a separate group of people who had stopped.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None reported: an overall mixed model, then 5 group contrasts in each of 6 regions separately for men and women (Tables 3 and 4, pp. 1866-1867).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The investigator who drew the regions of interest was unaware of the participant's history (p. 1866).

analysis.effect_sizes: Mixed model: group p=0.041, group-by-sex p=0.022 (p. 1866). Overall binding ratio differences, control minus group (Table 3, p. 1866): women, heavy use 0.168 (95% CI 0.078-0.259, p<0.01); men, heavy use 0.025 (-0.067 to 0.117, p=0.587); women, moderate use 0.058 (-0.046 to 0.162, p=0.269). Women who had stopped versus women with heavy use -0.137 (-0.227 to -0.046, p=0.004), i.e. higher binding in those who had stopped; versus controls 0.031 (-0.067 to 0.129, p=0.524). Regional results in women with heavy use versus controls (Table 4, p. 1866): midbrain 0.154 (0.034-0.274, p=0.013), thalamus 0.221 (0.022-0.421, p=0.030), frontal cortex 0.148 (0.073-0.223, p<0.01), temporal cortex 0.134 (0.006-0.262, p=0.040), parieto-occipital 0.177 (0.096-0.259, p<0.01), occipital 0.175 (0.090-0.260, p<0.01). In women who had stopped, binding was still non-significantly lower than in controls in the parieto-occipital (p=0.059) and occipital cortex (p=0.107). Correlation of overall binding with log lifetime tablets: women r=-0.33, p=0.048; men r=0.07, p=0.699 (p. 1867). No percentage changes are given; the outcome is a ratio.
analysis.covariates: Age and current depression added to the model; neither significant (age p=0.492, depression p=0.539) and neither changed the group effect (p. 1867).
analysis.selective_reporting: All six regions and both sexes are tabulated. The paper reports that excluding participants with depression did not change the result but gives no numbers ('data not shown', p. 1868).
analysis.power: A retrospective power calculation states that detecting the reduction seen in heavy use with 80% power would need 7 women but 393 men per group (pp. 1867-1868), so the null result in men is uninformative.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In one scan per person, women with heavy ecstasy use had lower [123I]beta-CIT binding ratios than women in the control group across all six regions; men did not differ; moderate use did not differ; and women who had stopped for a year or more had higher ratios than women currently using heavily and no significant difference from controls, with non-significant differences remaining in the two posterior cortical regions.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title and summary speak of 'toxic effects of MDMA on brain serotonin neurons' and conclude that heavy use 'is associated with neurotoxic effects on serotonin neurons' and that the MDMA-induced neurotoxic changes in several brain regions of the women who had stopped are reversible (summary, p. 1864). The results are a cross-sectional difference in a radioligand ratio between separately recruited groups: neither toxicity nor reversal was observed in anyone. The Discussion itself concedes that a prospective design would be needed to establish reversibility (p. 1868) and that pre-existing differences cannot be excluded (p. 1868).

timeline.event: First PET report of lower serotonin transporter binding in people who had used MDMA (McCann et al., Lancet 352:1433-1437), with a large global reduction later not replicated.
Quantitative PET with two radioligands finds lower binding, largest in cortex, and a positive association with time abstinent
Prospective SPECT with the same tracer in people who had just started using finds no difference in transporter binding
PET in men abstinent for at least a year finds no difference from controls
PET with a selective tracer and hair testing finds cortical and hippocampal reductions but normal striatum, and no sex difference in their size
PET finds reductions related to lifetime dose and a positive relation with time since last use in subcortical regions only
Review of molecular imaging counts 14 of 16 human studies with significantly lower transporter binding and judges the evidence on sex differences unsettled

replication.where_it_stands: Lower transporter binding in people who use ecstasy heavily is reported by several independent groups, but this study's two distinctive claims are not settled: the sex difference was not reproduced in the largest PET study (Kish et al., 2010, where reductions were of similar size in men and women), and 'reversibility' rests here and elsewhere on comparisons between different people at one time point.

funding.funder: Partly supported by a grant from the Netherlands Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sports (GVM grant 43894) (Acknowledgments, p. 1869).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement appears in the article (searched in the text extraction of all six pages).
funding.affiliations_note: Academic Medical Center, Amsterdam, and Leiden University Medical Center. The same group later ran the prospective NeXT cohort (de Win et al., 2008), which used the same tracer and found no transporter difference after low doses.

what_would_settle_it: Repeated scanning of the same people with a serotonin-selective tracer: before first use, during use and across years of abstinence, with a retested comparison group who do not start, biological verification of exposure, and enough men and women to test a sex difference rather than infer it from a null result in one sex.

domains.note: The ecstasy groups used more amphetamine (p=0.04) and cocaine (p=0.09) than controls; only age and depression were entered as covariates, and the model does not adjust for other drug use.

Lifetime tablets, dose and abstinence are self-reported, with one urine screen and no hair analysis; tablet content was not verified, and lifetime estimates reach hundreds of tablets with standard deviations larger than their means.
Four self-selected groups from one scene; the group that had stopped consists of people who used heavily and then stopped, which cannot be separated from any pre-existing difference.
One scan per person; no missing imaging data reported.

Region drawing was blinded and the measure is objective, but the tracer is not selective for the serotonin transporter and the outcome is a cerebellar ratio from a scanner with about 7.5 mm resolution.
Six regions, four groups and two sexes are reported without correction; one sensitivity analysis is reported without numbers.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A cross-sectional comparison of self-selected groups with unadjusted differences in other stimulant use and self-reported exposure. It can be cited for a group difference in a radioligand ratio and for the dose relation in women, not for causation, for the absence of an effect in men (power), or for recovery, which it did not observe within any person.

key_findings.finding: In the mixed model the overall effect of group (p=0.041) and the group-by-sex interaction (p=0.022) were significant, so all later comparisons are reported separately for men and women.

Overall binding ratio was lower in women with heavy use than in women in the control group (difference 0.168, 95% CI 0.078-0.259, p<0.01) but not in men (0.025, -0.067 to 0.117, p=0.587); moderate use did not differ in either sex (women 0.058, -0.046 to 0.162, p=0.269).
key_findings.note: The outcome is a ratio to cerebellar binding, so these are absolute differences in ratio units, not percentages; mean ratios are shown only in Figure 1 (p. 1866).

key_findings.finding: In women with heavy use, binding was lower than in controls in all six regions: midbrain 0.154 (0.034-0.274, p=0.013), thalamus 0.221 (0.022-0.421, p=0.030), frontal 0.148 (0.073-0.223, p<0.01), temporal 0.134 (0.006-0.262, p=0.040), parieto-occipital 0.177 (0.096-0.259, p<0.01), occipital 0.175 (0.090-0.260, p<0.01). In men no regional difference reached significance.

Women who had stopped for at least a year had higher overall binding than women with heavy use (-0.137, -0.227 to -0.046, p=0.004) and did not differ significantly from controls (0.031, -0.067 to 0.129, p=0.524); in the parieto-occipital (p=0.059) and occipital cortex (p=0.107) they remained non-significantly below controls.
key_findings.note: These are different people from the heavy-use group, scanned once: no one was followed over abstinence.

key_findings.finding: Overall binding correlated with log lifetime tablets in women (r=-0.33, p=0.048) but not men (r=0.07, p=0.699).
key_findings.note: The text extraction renders the coefficient as 'r=20.33'; the rendered page shows r=-0.33 (checked on the image of p. 1867).

key_findings.finding: A retrospective power calculation states that 7 women but 393 men per group would be needed to detect the reduction seen in heavy use with 80% power.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph on sex differences (begins p. 1867, the figures on p. 1868)
key_findings.note: The null result in men therefore bounds nothing; the paper nonetheless reads it as a sex difference.

key_findings.finding: Adding age and current depression to the model changed nothing (age p=0.492, depression p=0.539), and the four groups did not differ in verbal IQ, alcohol, tobacco or cannabis use, but ecstasy groups reported more amphetamine (p=0.04) and cocaine (p=0.09) use in the past 3 months.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives the sex difference in usual dose for the moderate group as 4.2 tablets with a 95% interval of -56.7 to 65.1, although the group's mean usual dose is 1.4 (SD 0.5) tablets.
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed interval cannot come from these data; the row is unusable and probably a misprint (the log transformation used for other variables is not stated for this row).

reporting_issues.issue: Also in Table 2, the sex difference in lifetime tablets per kg for the heavy group is -7.1 (95% CI -13.8 to -0.35) with p=0.06.
reporting_issues.consequence: An interval excluding zero with a p-value above 0.05 is internally inconsistent; one of the two is wrong.

reporting_issues.issue: The summary and title describe 'toxic effects on brain serotonin neurons' and reversibility, while the measurement is a [123I]beta-CIT binding ratio in groups scanned once, and the tracer also binds dopamine transporters.
reporting_issues.consequence: A surrogate marker and a between-group difference are presented as observed damage and observed recovery; the Discussion's own caveats (no prospective design, possible pre-existing differences) are not carried into the conclusions.

reporting_issues.issue: The null result in men is presented as a sex difference in susceptibility even though the paper's own power calculation shows the male comparison was powered only for an effect about 50 times larger per-group sample.
reporting_issues.consequence: Absence of a significant difference in men is not evidence of absence; the group-by-sex interaction (p=0.022) supports a difference in the estimates, but the regional male nulls carry no information.

reporting_issues.issue: Six regions, four groups and two sexes are compared without any correction for multiplicity, and one sensitivity analysis (excluding participants with depression) is reported only as 'data not shown'.
reporting_issues.consequence: Several of the regional p-values lie between 0.01 and 0.05 and would not survive correction; the unreported analysis cannot be checked.
